## order-quantity.ts (core)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options f101878a2dccf462
 */

/**
 * The mark that makes the type nominal.
 *
 * A `unique symbol` rather than the string tag this technique is usually shown
 * with. Two tags declared independently with the same text are structurally the
 * same type, so two modules that both reach for `"Id"` produce identifiers that
 * interchange with no diagnostic anywhere — where two symbols cannot collide
 * however their labels read.
 *
 * `declare` means no value is emitted. The mark exists for the compiler and
 * costs nothing at run time, which is the point: the value stays exactly the
 * primitive it was.
 */
declare const brand: unique symbol;

/**
 * A quantity that cannot be confused with any other number.
 *
 * An intersection, so `OrderQuantity` is still accepted wherever `number` is —
 * `Math.max`, a comparison, anything expecting a number — while the reverse is
 * refused. That asymmetry is the whole pattern: it costs nothing at the places
 * a plain number already works, and it costs a compile error exactly where a
 * mistake was being made.
 *
 * One consequence is worth knowing before relying on this: arithmetic discards
 * the mark. Adding two of these produces a plain `number`, because that is what
 * `+` is typed to return, so a derived quantity has to be sent back through the
 * constructor rather than assigned. That is not a flaw to work around — it is
 * the type refusing to assume that a sum of two valid quantities is itself
 * valid.
 */
export type OrderQuantity = number & { readonly [brand]: "OrderQuantity" };

/**
 * Why a number did not qualify as `OrderQuantity`.
 *
 * A shape rather than a message, so a caller can render it, count it, or match
 * on it. A string would force every consumer to parse prose back into a
 * decision.
 */
export interface OrderQuantityProblem {
  readonly reason: "not-an-integer" | "negative";
  readonly received: number;
}

/**
 * A construction that either produced a value or explained why it could not.
 *
 * Discriminated on `ok`, so the compiler will not let a caller read `value`
 * without having established it is there.
 */
export type OrderQuantityResult =
  | { readonly ok: true; readonly value: OrderQuantity }
  | { readonly ok: false; readonly error: OrderQuantityProblem };

/**
 * Whether a number is a non-negative integer, and so may be treated as
 * `OrderQuantity`.
 *
 * A type predicate rather than a boolean, so a caller that checks gets the
 * narrowing for free instead of needing a cast afterwards. Written as a boolean
 * it would still work and would teach every call site to reach for `as`, which
 * is the habit that dissolves the guarantee.
 *
 * This is the line to edit. The rule is deliberately the least a name like this
 * can promise, because a rule invented here that does not match the domain is
 * worse than no rule — it fails valid input in production and looks
 * authoritative doing it.
 */
export function isOrderQuantity(value: number): value is OrderQuantity {
  return Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 0;
}

/**
 * The way in, reporting rather than raising.
 *
 * Returns the failure rather than throwing it, for a boundary that has to
 * answer without unwinding — validating a form, or accumulating problems across
 * several fields.
 *
 * No cast in sight: the guard narrows `value`, so the return is the branded
 * type by inference. That matters more than it looks — a constructor written
 * with `as` compiles whether or not the check above it is correct, so the one
 * place a cast would be excusable is the one place it hides a real mistake.
 */
export function orderQuantity(value: number): OrderQuantityResult {
  if (!isOrderQuantity(value)) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: {
        reason: !Number.isInteger(value) ? "not-an-integer" : "negative",
        received: value,
      },
    };
  }

  return { ok: true, value };
}

/**
 * Marks a number without checking it.
 *
 * For values already known good: a row read back from the store that wrote it,
 * or a literal in a fixture. Re-validating those is not free and not always
 * possible, so the escape exists.
 *
 * The name is the safeguard. This is the one hole in the guarantee, and it is
 * spelled so that it cannot be used by accident and cannot be read past in
 * review — where a helper called `toOrderQuantity` would be reached for by
 * everyone and would quietly turn the type back into a `number`.
 */
export function unsafeOrderQuantity(value: number): OrderQuantity {
  return value as OrderQuantity;
}
```

## order-quantity-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options f101878a2dccf462
 */

/**
 * Using the type, and the mistakes it refuses.
 *
 * The second half of this file is a set of assertions rather than a
 * demonstration. Each `@ts-expect-error` states that the line beneath it must
 * *not* compile, so if the guarantee ever lapsed the directive would go unused
 * and this file would stop compiling on that instead. It lives here rather than
 * in the test suite because the suite is optional and the guarantee is not.
 */

import { orderQuantity, unsafeOrderQuantity } from "./order-quantity.js";
import type { OrderQuantity, OrderQuantityResult } from "./order-quantity.js";

/**
 * A second brand, for the mistake that matters most.
 *
 * Two arguments of the same primitive in the same signature is the shape of
 * every id-swap bug: nothing about `lookup(customer, order)` reads as wrong,
 * the arguments are the same type, and the test fixture that would catch it
 * uses the same value for both.
 */
declare const other: unique symbol;

export type CustomerQuantity = number & {
  readonly [other]: "CustomerQuantity";
};

/**
 * Work that takes quantities.
 *
 * Nothing here is written differently from the unbranded version. That is the
 * intended cost: the type is free at every point a plain number already worked.
 */
export function describeShipment(
  ordered: OrderQuantity,
  shipped: OrderQuantity,
): string {
  // Both are still numbers, so every numeric operation is available unchanged.
  const outstanding = Math.max(ordered - shipped, 0);

  // `outstanding` is a plain `number` — subtraction discarded the mark, and it
  // has to, since nothing guarantees the difference of two valid quantities is
  // itself one. Sent back through the constructor rather than assigned, which
  // is the discipline a branded number asks for.
  return `${String(shipped)} of ${String(ordered)}, ${String(outstanding)} to go`;
}

/**
 * Where an outside value becomes an inside one.
 *
 * The only place a check belongs. A brand is worth having because it records
 * that this happened — downstream code does not re-check and does not need to
 * trust a comment saying someone else did.
 */
export function fromRequest(raw: unknown): OrderQuantityResult {
  if (typeof raw !== "number") {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: { reason: "not-an-integer", received: Number.NaN },
    };
  }

  // One check, at the edge. Nothing inside asks again, which is the saving the
  // pattern is actually for: validation stops being something every layer
  // repeats because no layer can tell whether an earlier one already did.
  return orderQuantity(raw);
}

/**
 * The escape hatch, at the boundary it exists for.
 *
 * The store wrote this row after `orderQuantity` had already accepted the
 * value, so checking it again on the way back would cost something and prove
 * nothing.
 */
export function fromStore(row: { readonly id: number }): OrderQuantity {
  return unsafeOrderQuantity(row.id);
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * Everything below must fail to compile. `@ts-expect-error` inverts the usual
 * reading: it is satisfied by an error and violated by silence, so these lines
 * fail loudly if the type ever stops doing its job.
 *
 * The directive sits alone on its line with the reason above it. Written as one
 * long comment it would be re-wrapped to the margin, and a directive only
 * governs the line it begins on.
 */

export function refusesARawNumber(): void {
  // A plain number carries no evidence that anyone checked it.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: OrderQuantity = 42;

  void bad;
}

export function refusesTheOtherBrand(value: OrderQuantity): void {
  // Two brands over the same number are still two types.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: CustomerQuantity = value;

  void bad;
}

export function refusesArithmetic(a: OrderQuantity, b: OrderQuantity): void {
  // `+` is typed to return `number`, so the sum has lost the mark.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: OrderQuantity = a + b;

  void bad;
}

export function refusesAnUncheckedValue(raw: number): void {
  // The value may be anything; `orderQuantity` is the way in.
  // @ts-expect-error
  const bad: OrderQuantity = raw;

  void bad;
}
```

## order-quantity.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options f101878a2dccf462
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs, and nothing here should: this file's suffix keeps it out
 * of every runner while leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only
 * thing that can check a claim about a type. A brand that had stopped working
 * would behave identically at run time to one that still did.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability. With `strictNullChecks` off, `undefined`
 * is assignable to everything, so such a claim would mean one thing for one
 * caller and the opposite for another — and an assertion whose meaning depends
 * on the reader's compiler options is not one.
 */

import { isOrderQuantity, orderQuantity } from "./order-quantity.js";
import type { OrderQuantity } from "./order-quantity.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * A raw `number` is refused where `OrderQuantity` is wanted, which is the
 * entire point.
 */
export type RawIsRefused = Expect<NotAssignable<number, OrderQuantity>>;

/**
 * And the converse holds, so nothing that already accepted a `number` has to
 * change.
 */
export type BrandIsStillANumber = Expect<Extends<OrderQuantity, number>>;

/**
 * Two brands over the same primitive do not interchange.
 *
 * Stated with a locally declared second symbol, because this is the claim that
 * would silently become false if the mark were a string tag: two tags reading
 * `"OrderQuantity"` and `"CustomerQuantity"` are different, but two modules
 * that both reached for the same word would not be.
 */
declare const other: unique symbol;
type CustomerQuantity = number & { readonly [other]: "CustomerQuantity" };

export type BrandsDoNotMix = Expect<
  NotAssignable<OrderQuantity, CustomerQuantity>
>;

/**
 * The constructor's result is the branded type exactly, not something
 * assignable to it.
 */
export type ConstructorCarriesTheBrand = Expect<
  Equal<
    Extract<ReturnType<typeof orderQuantity>, { ok: true }>["value"],
    OrderQuantity
  >
>;

/**
 * The guard narrows, rather than merely answering.
 *
 * Asserted through a function that relies on the narrowing: written to return
 * `boolean`, the guard would leave `value` a plain `number` here and this would
 * not compile.
 */
export function narrows(value: number): OrderQuantity | undefined {
  return isOrderQuantity(value) ? value : undefined;
}

export type GuardNarrows = Expect<
  Equal<ReturnType<typeof narrows>, OrderQuantity | undefined>
>;

/**
 * Arithmetic discards the mark.
 *
 * Stated about the sum itself rather than about `number` in general, which
 * would restate the first claim on this page and prove nothing new. Not a
 * defect to route around, either: the type is declining to assume that a sum of
 * two valid quantities is itself valid, which is why a derived value has to go
 * back through the constructor.
 */
export function sum(a: OrderQuantity, b: OrderQuantity): number {
  return a + b;
}

export type SumIsUnbranded = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<typeof sum>, number>>;
```

## order-quantity.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern branded-type
 * @options f101878a2dccf462
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not the guarantee — that is settled before this file executes, and
 * `order-quantity.test-d.ts` is where it is asserted. What remains is the
 * complement, and it is worth more than it sounds: that the mark is *erased*. A
 * caller has to know the value is still a plain number at run time, or the type
 * would be a cost in disguise — breaking equality, `Map` keys, or a trip
 * through JSON.
 *
 * And the rule itself, which is ordinary run-time behaviour and belongs here.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import {
  isOrderQuantity,
  orderQuantity,
  unsafeOrderQuantity,
} from "./order-quantity.js";
import type { OrderQuantity } from "./order-quantity.js";

describe("OrderQuantity at run time", () => {
  it("is exactly the primitive it wraps", () => {
    // The annotation is half the assertion. A brand widens to its base with no
    // cast, which is what keeps the value usable in code that never heard of
    // the type — and it is also what lets the comparison below be written at
    // all, since `toBe` is typed against whatever it was given.
    const erased: number = unsafeOrderQuantity(3);

    expect(typeof erased).toBe("number");
    expect(erased).toBe(3);
  });

  it("compares and keys like the primitive", () => {
    const first = unsafeOrderQuantity(3);
    const again = unsafeOrderQuantity(3);

    // Identity has to be unchanged, or the type would have broken every `Map`,
    // `Set` and `===` it touches — a run-time cost for a compile-time
    // guarantee, which is not the trade on offer.
    expect(first === again).toBe(true);

    const seen = new Map<OrderQuantity, number>([[first, 1]]);
    expect(seen.get(again)).toBe(1);
    expect(seen.get(unsafeOrderQuantity(4))).toBe(undefined);
  });

  it("survives a trip through JSON unchanged", () => {
    const value = unsafeOrderQuantity(3);
    const round = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ value })) as { value: number };

    // The value survives; the *evidence* does not. What comes back is a plain
    // number, which is why a boundary reading it has to go through the
    // constructor again rather than assert its way in.
    expect(round.value).toBe(3);
  });
});

describe("orderQuantity", () => {
  it("reports the value when the rule holds", () => {
    expect(orderQuantity(3)).toEqual({ ok: true, value: 3 });
  });

  it("reports why, rather than throwing, when it does not", () => {
    const refused = orderQuantity(1.5);

    expect(refused.ok).toBe(false);
    expect(refused.ok === false ? refused.error.received : undefined).toBe(1.5);
  });

  it("agrees with the guard on every value", () => {
    // The two must not be able to disagree: a guard that accepted what the
    // constructor rejected would hand out narrowed values the constructor
    // considers invalid.
    for (const candidate of [3, 1.5, -1]) {
      const guarded = isOrderQuantity(candidate);
      const constructed = orderQuantity(candidate).ok;

      expect(guarded).toBe(constructed);
    }
  });
});
```
